map.title: Map of the internet
map.lead: Every network of the internet and the links between them, rebuilt every night from open routing data. Enter two addresses: the map draws the way packets are likely to go — network by network, where they meet and how long it takes.
map.description: An interactive map of the internet: 80 thousand networks, the links between them and the exchange points where they meet. Trace the likely route between any two IP addresses.

views.label: View
views.core_hint: The core: the largest networks in the middle, the smallest on the rim; the angle is where on Earth they are.

panel.note: The path is what the routing policies of the networks make likely; the delay is estimated from the distance along the cables, the ports are what the networks declare in PeeringDB. Real routers may choose another way, and loss can only be measured.

about.heading: How it works
paragraphs: The internet is some 80 thousand autonomous systems — providers, hosting, clouds, companies — and each decides whom to connect to and whose traffic to carry. They tell each other about it with BGP. Collectors that many networks talk BGP to keep their tables open: from them, from CAIDA's research into the kinds of links and from PeeringDB, where networks tell where they can be met, the map is rebuilt every night. Only what changed is written: new links, and links that went away.

A route is the chain of networks their policies make likely: a network would rather hand traffic to a customer, who pays, than to a peer, and to a peer rather than to its own provider. Where two networks meet is seen from the exchange points and data centres they share. The delay is estimated from the distance: light in fibre covers about 200 km in a millisecond, and cables are longer than straight lines.
Real routers may choose another way, and loss can only be measured. Measurements are coming: traceroute from this site's server and, through RIPE Atlas, from a probe in the sender's own network.
